common_name: Lady Vanessa Siberian Iris (Wine-Red Morgan-Wood Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Lady Vanessa bears light wine-red standards over ruffled, deeper wine-red falls with a faint white signal.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Robert Hollingworth from 'Ruffled Velvet' and 'Showdown', Lady Vanessa carries light wine-red standards with feathered style arms over heavily ruffled, deeper wine-red falls marked by only a faint white signal, a rich two-tone wine effect that earned it the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 1992. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a good choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go several years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or just after spring bloom.

common_name: Here Be Dragons Siberian Iris (Yellow Bitone with Blue-Violet Overlay)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Here Be Dragons bears pale yellow standards over deep yellow falls heavily overlaid with blue-violet veining.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Registered by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks from 'Sarah Tiffney' crossed with 'Tom Schaefer', Here Be Dragons shows pale yellow standards above style arms that deepen toward blue-violet hearts, while the dark yellow falls are washed and lightly veined blue-violet with a warm yellow signal, a striking bitone combination recognized with the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2010. It is slightly fragrant and a notably free-blooming, early-midseason grower. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer or right after bloom to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Judy, Judy, Judy Siberian Iris (Tetraploid Red-Violet Plicata)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Judy, Judy, Judy is a tetraploid Siberian iris with medium red-violet standards over white, plicata-dotted falls.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Robert Hollingworth as a tetraploid sibling to 'Currier' and 'Somebody Loves Me', Judy, Judy, Judy pairs medium red-violet standards and light blue style arms with white falls stippled in red-violet dots that merge into an outer plicata band, a pattern distinctive enough to earn the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2017. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a good choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go several years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or just after spring bloom.

common_name: Cape Cod Boys Siberian Iris (Dappled Blue-Violet Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Cape Cod Boys bears dappled blue-violet flowers with a gold-to-pale-yellow signal and can rebloom later in the season.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks, Cape Cod Boys carries blue-violet standards and falls heavily dappled and veined in a deeper blue-violet, edged with a paler rim and centered on a gold-to-pale-yellow signal lightly veined blue-violet, a lightly fragrant pattern that won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2021. Unlike many Siberian iris cultivars it reliably reblooms later in the season under good growing conditions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer or right after bloom to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Where Eagles Dare Siberian Iris (Dark Violet-Blue Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Where Eagles Dare is a tall, dark violet-blue Siberian iris with a gold-touched white signal.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Hybridized by Calvin Helsley from 'Mabel Coday' and a seedling tracing back to 'Marlya' and 'Steve', Where Eagles Dare is a tall, dark violet-blue self with slightly darker veining and a white signal that turns gold in the throat, a striking deep-colored form that earned the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2005. At up to 41 inches it is taller than most Siberian iris cultivars, giving good presence at the back of a mixed border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer or right after bloom to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Lake Keuka Siberian Iris (Ruffled Violet-Blue with Aqua Styles)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Lake Keuka bears ruffled violet-blue flowers with distinctive aqua-toned style arms.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Dana Borglum from 'Gulls Way' and 'Outer Loop', Lake Keuka pairs violet-blue, ruffled falls edged lighter with unusual aqua-toned style arms, a cool color combination that earned repeated Favorite Guest Iris honors before taking the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2002. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a good choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go several years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or just after spring bloom.

common_name: Frosted Cranberry Siberian Iris (Red-Violet with Aqua Veining)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Frosted Cranberry bears deep red-violet flowers accented with unusual aqua veining and blooms into late season.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Anna Mae Miller from a 'Pink Haze' lineage, Frosted Cranberry carries red-violet standards laced with aqua veins over darker red-violet falls with greenish hafts and signal, a cranberry-toned color break that won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 1998. It blooms later than many Siberian iris cultivars, extending midseason into late bloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer or right after bloom to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Art In Bloom Siberian Iris (Blue-Violet and Yellow Bitone, 2026 Morgan-Wood Medal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Art In Bloom pairs bright blue-violet standards with a yellow-ground, blue-violet-veined fall.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks with a complex pedigree running through 'Summer Revels', 'Tom Schaefer', and 'Tipped In Blue', Art In Bloom shows bright blue-violet, darker-veined standards over a yellow-ground fall overlaid with blue-violet veining and wash and finished with a narrow yellow rim and blaze, a lightly fragrant bitone pattern that earned the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2026. It is a strong grower that typically sends up multiple branched stalks carrying several buds per stem. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer or right after bloom to keep plants vigorous.
